title: “GOD IS TREATING YOU AS SONS” — WHAT IF THE PAIN YOU THOUGHT WAS GOD REJECTING YOU IS WHERE HE IS TEACHING YOU TO TRUST HIM?
paragraphs: “GOD IS TREATING YOU AS SONS” — WHAT IF THE PAIN YOU THOUGHT WAS GOD REJECTING YOU IS WHERE HE IS TEACHING YOU TO TRUST HIM?

Hebrews 12 reveals a difficult truth about the Father's love: God does not abandon His children to the things that are destroying them. But before you call every painful season His discipline, you need to understand what Scripture actually says.
There is a kind of pain that makes you question whether God still loves you.
Not the pain you talk about at church.
Not the kind you can easily turn into a testimony because everything has already worked out.
I'm talking about the pain that follows you into your bedroom when everyone else is asleep.
The prayers you have repeated so many times that you have started wondering whether heaven is listening.
The doors that closed after you begged God to open them.
The temptation you promised you would never return to.
The consequences of decisions you desperately wish you could undo.
The private exhaustion of trying to live faithfully while everything around you seems to be falling apart.
And somewhere in that darkness, a frightening thought enters your mind.
Maybe God is disappointed in me.
Then another.
Maybe He is punishing me.
And finally, the thought that hurts most.
Maybe He doesn't want me anymore.
But what if the passage you have been afraid to read contains an answer you desperately need to hear?
What if Hebrews 12 is not the portrait of an angry Father looking for reasons to reject His children, but of a holy Father who loves them too deeply to leave them unchanged?
There is one sentence in this chapter that can completely transform how you understand God's discipline.
And once you see what it means in its original context, you may never read your difficult seasons quite the same way again.
“God is treating you as sons.” — Hebrews 12:7, ESV
Read that again.
Not as enemies.
Not as strangers.
Not as unwanted burdens.
As sons.
And in the world of Hebrews, that word carries a depth of belonging that our modern ears can easily miss.
The Greek text of Hebrews 12:7 reads:
εἰς παιδείαν ὑπομένετε· ὡς υἱοῖς ὑμῖν προσφέρεται ὁ θεός.
Eis paideian hypomenete; hōs huiois hymin prospheretai ho theos.
A faithful rendering is:
“It is for discipline that you have to endure. God is treating you as sons.” (ESV)
The word translated “discipline” is παιδεία — paideia.
And this is where many people misunderstand the passage.
Paideia is not limited to punishment.
It includes the education, upbringing, instruction, correction, and formation of a child.
It describes the process through which a parent trains a child toward maturity.
Sometimes that training involves correction.
Sometimes it involves learning endurance.
Sometimes it means confronting destructive behavior.
And sometimes it means growing through hardship that was never caused by a particular personal sin.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because if you believe every painful experience is God punishing you, you may begin accusing Him of things Scripture never attributes to Him.
A diagnosis is not automatically divine punishment.
Losing someone you love does not prove that God is angry with you.
Being betrayed does not mean you deserved betrayal.
Experiencing abuse does not mean God arranged your suffering to teach you a lesson.
Jesus Himself rejected the assumption that suffering always results from someone's particular sin (John 9:1–3).
And Hebrews 12 does not give us permission to explain every tragedy as a specific act of divine discipline.
But it does reveal something astonishing.
For those who belong to Christ, suffering does not have the authority to cancel their relationship with the Father.
God can form His children through hardship without being the author of every evil they experience.
He can bring redemption out of what others intended for destruction.
And He can lovingly correct what would otherwise lead them away from life.
That is not cruelty.
That is the kind of love that refuses to surrender a child to destruction.
But there is something even more powerful hidden in the passage.
Hebrews 12 does not begin with a command to stare at your pain.
It begins by telling you where to look.
“Looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith.” — Hebrews 12:2, ESV
Before the writer explains the Father's discipline, he directs suffering believers to the Son.
To Jesus.
The One who endured the cross.
The One who was publicly humiliated.
The One who was mocked, rejected, wounded, and crucified.
The One who experienced suffering without ever committing sin.
And that changes everything.
Because if suffering automatically meant God had rejected someone, how would we understand the cross?
Jesus was the beloved Son, yet He suffered.
He was perfectly obedient, yet He was persecuted.
He was without sin, yet He endured unimaginable injustice.
His suffering was not the Father's punishment for sins Jesus had committed.
He had none.
Instead, in the mystery of God's saving purpose, the sinless Christ bore our sins and gave Himself for our redemption (1 Peter 2:24).
The cross destroys the lie that pain, by itself, proves the absence of God's love.
And the resurrection destroys the lie that suffering gets the final word.
Maybe you need to hear that tonight.
Because you have been interpreting God's love through your circumstances instead of interpreting your circumstances in light of what God has revealed through Jesus Christ.
When life feels good, you believe He loves you.
When prayers are answered, you believe He is near.
When blessings arrive, you believe He approves of you.
But when everything becomes difficult, you begin questioning the very love Christ demonstrated at Calvary.
Listen carefully.
The cross is not evidence that every hardship will end the way you want.
It is evidence that God's saving love is deeper than the suffering you can presently understand.
Romans 8:32 asks:
“He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (ESV)
And later, that same chapter declares that neither death nor life, nor anything else in creation, can separate those in Christ Jesus from God's love.
Not even the season you are barely surviving.
Not even the tears nobody knows about.
Not even the struggle that makes you wonder whether you will ever feel strong again.
But we must go deeper.
Because Hebrews 12 is not merely telling us that God comforts His children.
It is also telling us that He corrects them.
And that is where the passage becomes uncomfortable.
Hebrews 12:5–6 quotes the wisdom of Proverbs:
“My son, do not regard lightly the discipline of the Lord, nor be weary when reproved by him. For the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and chastises every son whom he receives.” (ESV)
The original Hebrew of Proverbs 3:12 begins:
כִּי אֶת־אֲשֶׁר יֶאֱהַב יְהוָה יוֹכִיחַ
Ki et-asher ye'ehav Adonai yokhiach.
“For the LORD reproves him whom he loves...” (Proverbs 3:12, ESV)
The Hebrew verb יוֹכִיחַ — yokhiach, from the root יכח (y-k-ḥ), carries the sense of correcting, reproving, or bringing someone to recognize what is right.
Notice the relationship.
Love and correction are not presented as opposites.
God's correction flows from His covenantal concern for His people.
The biblical picture is not of a Father who enjoys seeing His children suffer.
It is of a Father who is committed to their holiness.
And holiness is not a decorative religious word.
It means belonging to God.
Being set apart for Him.
Learning to turn away from what corrupts the soul and toward what reflects His character.
That process can be painful because sin does not always feel destructive when we first embrace it.
Sometimes sin feels like relief.
Sometimes pride feels like strength.
Sometimes bitterness feels like justice.
Sometimes revenge feels like healing.
Sometimes lust feels like intimacy.
Sometimes greed feels like security.
Sometimes spiritual compromise feels like the easiest way to survive.
And sometimes the very thing we keep asking God to bless is the thing that is slowly pulling our hearts away from Him.
That is why divine correction is not something to dismiss.
There are moments when the most merciful answer God can give is not permission to continue.
It is a call to repent.
Think about the prodigal son.
He wanted his father's inheritance without his father's presence.
He wanted freedom without accountability.
Pleasure without consequences.
A life where nobody could tell him what to do.
And for a while, it probably felt wonderful.
Until the money disappeared.
Until the friends disappeared.
Until the hunger became unbearable.
Until he found himself longing for the food given to pigs.
Then Luke 15:17 records a remarkable turning point.
“But when he came to himself...” (ESV)
What a sentence.
He came to himself.
Not because he had finally discovered how to justify his choices.
Not because he had learned to blame everyone else.
But because the illusion was breaking.
He could finally see what his rebellion had cost him.
And he remembered his father.
Somebody reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You remember when prayer used to be natural.
When opening your Bible did not feel like a burden.
When worship was not just music playing in the background.
When your conscience was tender.
When you could recognize compromise before it became a habit.
But somewhere along the way, you started negotiating with things you once resisted.
You became comfortable with what used to convict you.
And now you are exhausted from maintaining a version of yourself that looks spiritually alive while privately struggling to breathe.
You smile in church.
You encourage other people.
You share verses.
You tell everyone you are fine.
But God knows what happens after you put the phone down.
He knows what you have been hiding.
He knows what you have been feeding.
He knows what you have been grieving.
And He knows how tired you are of pretending.
The answer is not to hide more skillfully.
It is to come home.
Because the most beautiful part of the prodigal son's story is not that the son finally understood his sin.
It is what happened when he returned.
Luke 15:20 says:
“But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him.” (ESV)
The father did not celebrate the rebellion.
He did not pretend the sin was harmless.
He did not say the wasted years were wise.
But he welcomed his repentant son.
That is grace.
Not the denial of sin.
Not permission to remain enslaved to it.
But undeserved mercy that receives the repentant and opens the way to restoration.
And the Gospel gives us something even greater than a parable.
It gives us Jesus Christ, through whom sinners are reconciled to the Father.
Here is the truth many wounded believers need to recover.
God's discipline is not the price you pay to purchase His love.
You cannot buy that love through suffering.
You cannot earn salvation by surviving enough hardship.
You cannot punish yourself into becoming acceptable to God.
Ephesians 2:8–9 tells us that salvation is by grace through faith, not by works.
Jesus has already accomplished what our moral effort could never accomplish.
And for those who are united to Him by faith, Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.” (ESV)
No condemnation.
That does not mean no correction.
It does not mean no consequences.
It does not mean no painful confrontation with sin.
It means the believer's relationship with God is no longer defined by the condemnation Christ bore on our behalf.
A loving Father's correction is not the same thing as a condemning Judge's final sentence.
And confusing those two can turn the Christian life into a prison of fear.
Maybe you have been treating every setback as proof that God has withdrawn His mercy.
Maybe you have been interpreting every difficulty as evidence that you are beyond forgiveness.
Maybe you have spent years trying to become worthy of a grace that was never offered as a reward for perfection.
But the Gospel does not say, “Make yourself flawless, and then come to Jesus.”
It says to repent and believe in Him.
To confess rather than conceal.
To turn from sin rather than defend it.
To trust the Savior who died and rose again.
And to walk in the new life His Spirit produces.
That is why Hebrews 12:10 says that God disciplines His children “for our good, that we may share his holiness.” (ESV)
Not for His amusement.
Not because He delights in humiliation.
Not because He needs to crush your personality.
For our good.
And then comes one of the most painfully honest verses in the chapter.
Hebrews 12:11:
“For the moment all discipline seems painful rather than pleasant, but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.” (ESV)
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not say discipline feels wonderful.
It does not say mature believers never cry.
It does not say you must smile through every loss.
It does not say that grief is unbelief.
It admits that discipline is painful.
The Greek word λυπηρᾶς — lypēras describes what is grievous or distressing.
And the writer does not apologize for that reality.
Faith is not pretending something does not hurt.
Faith is trusting God without requiring yourself to deny that it does.
You can love Jesus and still weep.
You can trust His promises and still need help.
You can believe in His goodness and still struggle to understand what is happening.
Even Jesus wept at the tomb of Lazarus.
Even Jesus prayed in Gethsemane with deep anguish.
Christian maturity is not emotional numbness.
It is growing in faithful dependence on God through the full reality of being human.
But notice another word in Hebrews 12:11.
γεγυμνασμένοις — gegymnasmenois.
It comes from the Greek verb gymnazō, meaning to train or exercise.
It is related to the idea of athletic training.
The verse describes those who have been trained by discipline.
Not merely those who have experienced pain.
That difference is important.
Pain by itself does not automatically produce holiness.
Some suffering leaves people wounded, angry, frightened, or isolated.
And those wounds may require patient care, wise counsel, practical support, and time.
The fruit Hebrews describes belongs to God's gracious work of training His children.
The goal is not suffering for suffering's sake.
The goal is the peaceful fruit of righteousness.
A life increasingly shaped by what is right before God.
A heart learning obedience.
A conscience becoming sensitive to truth.
A person growing in endurance, humility, and love.
And sometimes the first evidence of that growth is not a dramatic breakthrough.
Sometimes it is a quiet confession.
“Lord, I was wrong.”
Sometimes it is finally telling someone you need help.
Sometimes it is deleting the message you were about to send in anger.
Sometimes it is refusing to return to a destructive relationship.
Sometimes it is seeking accountability for an addiction.
Sometimes it is choosing forgiveness while still establishing necessary boundaries.
Sometimes it is opening your Bible after months of avoiding it.
Sometimes it is praying five honest words.
“Jesus, I need You again.”
And perhaps that is where you are right now.
Not standing triumphantly on a mountain.
Not celebrating an answered prayer.
Not holding a beautiful testimony with a perfectly resolved ending.
Just sitting in the middle of an unfinished story.
Wondering whether God can still do something beautiful with the pieces.
He can.
But not because every broken thing automatically becomes a blessing.
And not because every consequence disappears when you repent.
Some choices leave scars.
Some relationships are not restored.
Some opportunities never return.
Some losses remain painful for the rest of this earthly life.
The Gospel does not promise that every earthly story will end the way we would have written it.
It promises something greater.
Through Jesus Christ, forgiveness is real.
Reconciliation with God is possible.
The Holy Spirit renews those who belong to Christ.
And resurrection means that death itself will not have the final word over God's redeemed people.
That is the hope we are holding.
Not a promise of an easy life.
A promise anchored in a risen Savior.
And there is another detail in Hebrews 12 that deserves our attention.
The chapter was written to believers who were growing weary.
They had endured hostility and hardship.
Earlier, Hebrews 10:32–34 recalls their suffering, public mistreatment, and loss of possessions.
They were not simply being told to stop behaving badly.
They were being encouraged to endure faithfully in a hostile world.
This is why Hebrews 12:3 says to consider Jesus, “so that you may not grow weary or fainthearted.” (ESV)
The writer knows that faithful people can become exhausted.
And instead of telling them that exhaustion proves they are not God's children, he calls them to remember Christ.
The Father has not forgotten them.
Their endurance matters.
Their holiness matters.
Their faith matters.
And their suffering does not mean that their inheritance in Christ has disappeared.
In fact, the Greek word υἱοῖς — huiois, translated “sons,” points to their standing as children in a family.
In the ancient setting, sonship was closely connected with recognized family status and inheritance.
The New Testament extends this inheritance in Christ to all believers, male and female.
Galatians 3:26–29 makes that clear.
Through faith in Christ Jesus, believers belong to God's family and share in the promise.
So when Hebrews says God is treating believers as sons, it is not telling women that they are excluded.
It is using the language of recognized children and heirs to emphasize the dignity of belonging to God.
Think about that.
The One who formed the galaxies is not merely tolerating His redeemed people.
He has brought them into His family through Jesus Christ.
He calls them to holiness because they belong to Him.
And that belonging changes the meaning of correction.
But we must also confront something that has harmed many people.
Hebrews 12 has sometimes been used to excuse harsh parenting, spiritual intimidation, abusive relationships, and religious leaders who demand unquestioning submission.
That is a misuse of Scripture.
God's fatherly discipline must never become an excuse for human cruelty.
The passage does not authorize anyone to abuse, humiliate, threaten, or control another person in God's name.
Earthly parents and spiritual leaders are accountable to God's commands.
Ephesians 6:4 specifically warns fathers not to provoke their children to anger but to raise them in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.
And Jesus taught that spiritual leadership must not imitate the domineering behavior of worldly rulers (Mark 10:42–45).
If someone is hurting you and calling it God's discipline, you do not have to accept that interpretation.
Seeking safety and appropriate help is not rebellion against God.
The Father revealed through Jesus Christ is not a license for abusers to claim divine authority.
His holiness never makes evil good.
And His love never requires us to call cruelty righteousness.
This matters because some readers do not struggle to believe God is powerful.
They struggle to believe He is safe to approach.
Perhaps the word father brings painful memories.
Perhaps the person who should have protected you was the person who frightened you.
Perhaps correction in your childhood meant humiliation rather than guidance.
And when you read Hebrews 12, you instinctively imagine God behaving like the person who wounded you.
But the character of God is not defined by the failures of human fathers.
Jesus reveals the Father to us (John 14:9).
And the God who welcomes repentant sinners, defends the vulnerable, commands justice, and gives His Son for our salvation is not merely a larger version of a flawed human parent.
He is holy.
He is righteous.
He is merciful.
And His fatherly love is not corrupted by the selfishness that so often damages earthly relationships.
Perhaps learning to trust Him will take time.
Perhaps you need to bring your questions, grief, and memories into prayer.
Perhaps you need the support of wise believers and qualified counselors.
There is no shame in that.
Healing does not always happen in one dramatic moment.
And spiritual growth is not measured by how quickly you can make painful memories disappear.
Sometimes grace works patiently.
Quietly.
Deeply.
One truthful step at a time.
And now we arrive at the part of Hebrews 12 that many readers overlook.
After discussing discipline, the writer says:
What an extraordinary command.
He does not say, “You are weak, so you are worthless.”
He does not say, “You are struggling, so give up.”
He calls weary believers to renewed strength.
Then he urges them to pursue peace and holiness.
The purpose of this passage is not to leave God's children crushed beneath fear.
It is to strengthen them for faithful endurance.
To turn their eyes back toward Jesus.
To remind them that their Father is forming them for something greater than immediate comfort.
And to call them to keep walking.
So perhaps the question tonight is not simply, “Why am I suffering?”
Perhaps it is also:
“Lord, how can I remain faithful to You here?”
“What sin do I need to confess?”
“What truth have I been resisting?”
“What help do I need to seek?”
“What obedience have I been postponing?”
“What false picture of You do I need to surrender?”
And sometimes the most faithful prayer will be:
“Father, I do not understand this suffering. Please comfort me, sustain me, and help me trust You.”
You do not have to invent an explanation for every wound.
You do not have to pretend that every tragedy was a personal lesson.
You do not have to force yourself to feel grateful for evil.
But you can bring the whole truth of your life to Jesus.
The sin.
The grief.
The confusion.
The regret.
The anger.
The unanswered questions.
The exhaustion.
All of it.
Because the Gospel is not about hiding our brokenness until we become presentable.
It is about coming to the Savior who alone can forgive, cleanse, restore, and make us new.
And if you have wandered far from God, hear the invitation of Christ.
Repent.
Turn toward Him.
Not because your tears are enough to pay for your sins.
Not because your promises can guarantee that you will never fail again.
But because Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose again.
Because His mercy is real.
Because forgiveness is offered through Him.
Because grace does not merely cover our past; it also calls us into a transformed life.
That is not a promise that the world will forget everything you have done.
It is the proclamation that your sin does not have to be the final authority over your identity and destiny.
Peter denied Jesus three times.
Yet the risen Christ restored him and entrusted him with the care of His sheep (John 21:15–19).
Paul persecuted the church.
Yet Christ showed him mercy and made him a servant of the Gospel (1 Timothy 1:12–16).
The prodigal son squandered his inheritance.
Yet his father welcomed him home when he returned.
Their stories were not rewritten by pretending their sins never happened.
They were transformed by mercy.
And the same Jesus who restored sinners then is still mighty to save.
Maybe you are reading this with tears in your eyes.
Maybe you are thinking about something you have never told anyone.
Maybe you are tired of carrying the weight of a secret.
Maybe you have been trying to outrun conviction because you are terrified of what repentance might require.
But hear this.
The conviction that calls you to Christ is not an invitation to despair.
It is an invitation to come into the light.
First John 1:9 reminds believers that when we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
Not because sin is insignificant.
But because Jesus Christ is sufficient.
And if you are already in Christ but are walking through a painful season, remember this:
Your suffering does not make you an orphan.
Your weakness does not surprise your Father.
Your tears do not cancel His promises.
And your unfinished growth does not mean His grace has failed.
The One who began a good work in His people will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ (Philippians 1:6).
That promise is not permission to become passive.
It is courage to keep trusting, repenting, obeying, and depending on Him.
Even when the road is long.
Even when the healing is slow.
Even when the answer has not come.
Even when you are still learning how to pray through tears.
And now I want to ask you something personal.
Not as someone who has everything figured out.
Not as someone who has never struggled.
But as one human being speaking to another beneath the mercy of God.
What have you been calling rejection that might actually be a moment to return to the Father?
Perhaps there is a sin He is calling you to abandon.
Perhaps there is a truth He is teaching you to trust.
Perhaps there is a wound that needs care rather than condemnation.
Perhaps there is a difficult season in which He is calling you to endure without losing sight of Christ.
Or perhaps you simply need to stop assuming that your pain means you are unloved.
You do not need to disclose private details publicly.
You do not have to tell your whole story to be worthy of compassion.
Sometimes a few honest words are enough to remind another struggling believer that they are not alone.
And if you have a testimony of how God used His Word to correct, restore, or strengthen you, consider sharing it.
Not to glorify suffering.
Not to make yourself the hero.
But to testify to the faithfulness of Jesus Christ.
Someone else may be one honest testimony away from finding the courage to open their Bible again.
Someone may have quietly decided that God could never welcome them back.
Someone may be carrying shame so heavy that they have forgotten what grace means.
Your words may help point them toward the Savior.
And that is also why I want to ask you to do something beyond reading this article.
Not merely to increase its reach.
Somebody may need to understand the difference between divine correction and condemnation.
Somebody may need to discover that repentance is not the end of hope but the beginning of returning to Christ.
You do not need to expose anyone's struggles.
Sometimes a simple, “This reminded me of God's faithfulness,” is enough.
Not because every sentence will apply to every season, but because Hebrews 12 is a passage worth returning to when your emotions begin telling you that God has forgotten you.
Read the chapter for yourself.
Study it in context.
Look again at Jesus.
Let Scripture, not fear, shape your understanding of the Father's love.
If you have not yet followed Gospel Warrior, I warmly invite you to join us.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, those who have grown distant from church, and even those who are still searching for the truth about Jesus.
Our desire is to keep pointing people toward Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, healing, and authentic discipleship in Christ.
Not toward a personality.
Not toward religious performance.
Toward Jesus.
There is a real mission behind the words you read here.

Writing Scripture-centered messages, developing discipleship materials, expanding our Christian resource library, and reaching more people with the Gospel all require ongoing time, effort, and resources.
For those who have been looking for a practical way to support Christian teaching and Gospel outreach, this is one meaningful opportunity.

Scripture teaches that believers may generously support those who minister the Word (Galatians 6:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14) and that Christian giving should be willing rather than pressured (2 Corinthians 9:7).
You cannot purchase His approval.
And your access to His grace will never depend on a monthly payment.
That support matters.
Especially when it helps biblical teaching reach people who may never be able to pay for it themselves.
We want that library to continue growing.
We want more people to have access to biblical nourishment.
We want struggling believers to find encouragement grounded in Scripture.
We want seekers to encounter the truth of the Gospel.
And we want to keep reminding wounded people that Jesus Christ offers something this world cannot manufacture.
Redemption.
Those items can serve as everyday reminders of faith, opportunities for Gospel conversations, and thoughtful gifts for people you love.
It is the opportunity to help sustain a ministry committed to keeping Jesus Christ and His Word at the center.
You can still pray for this ministry.
You can still make use of the free resources.
You can still encourage someone who is struggling.
Jesus Christ is the treasure.
Everything we do should point back to Him.
And before you leave, I want you to return to that one sentence from Hebrews.
“God is treating you as sons.”
Not because every hardship is a punishment.
Not because God enjoys your tears.
Not because you have to suffer enough to earn a place in His family.
But because, through faith in Jesus Christ, believers are received as God's children, and their Father is committed to their growth in holiness.
He does not promise a painless journey.
He promises that His saving purpose in Christ will not fail.
So if He is correcting you, do not harden your heart.
Repent and receive His mercy.
If you are suffering unjustly, do not blame yourself for another person's sin.
Seek help, pursue what is right, and bring your grief to Him.
If you are weary, do not confuse exhaustion with abandonment.
Look to Jesus.
And if you have wandered, do not wait until you feel worthy enough to return.
Come to Christ.
Today.
With the truth.
With the tears.
With the sins you need to confess.
With the questions you cannot yet answer.
With the faith you are struggling to hold.
Because the Father who calls His children to holiness is the same Father who gave His beloved Son to save sinners.
And the Savior who endured the cross is the risen Lord who calls His people to follow Him.
That is the love hidden inside Hebrews 12's difficult teaching.
Not a sentimental love that ignores sin.
Not a cruel love that delights in suffering.
But a holy, redeeming love that calls us out of darkness and teaches us to walk in the light.
So do not let your pain write the final sentence of your story.
Do not let your shame name you.
Do not let your past convince you that the cross was insufficient.
Look to Jesus.
Trust His Word.
Receive His grace.
And keep walking with the Father.
Because the hands that were pierced to redeem you are the reason your broken story does not have to end where your shame began.
